To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The Li-Fraumenii Syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition characterized by the development of a variety of tumour types, particularly sarcomas, breast cancer and brain tumours, at a young age.
We have analysed Li Fraumeni syndrome families that have been previously shown to be wild type for the TP53 gene for mutations to two other tumour suppressor gene, CDKN2 and PTEM.
we have excluded the CDKN2 and the PTEN genes in a series of 10 Li-Fraumenie families.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genes that are mutated in familial breast cancer.
the identification of the genetic basis of cancer predisposition syndromes and in particular with the identification of genes that predispose to breast cancer.
the genetic basis of cancer and the identification of genes involved in the development of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Li-Fraumenie syndrome is a disease of TP53.
mutations in the genes TP53, CDKN2, PTEN and MSH2 are not the underlying cause of Li-Fraumenie syndrome in these families.
the Li-Fraumenii families tested do not have a germline mutation in TP53, PTEN or CDKN2, and that the TP53 mutation is likely to be the only causative defect in Li-Fraumani syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
TP53 mutations account for most Li-Fraumenii families.
we have excluded mutations in TP53 in 11 of our 13 Li-Fraumenis syndrome families.
the Li-Fraumenis syndrome tumour phenotype is unlikely to be caused by mutations in these genes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mutations in PTEN and CDNK2 are not the cause of Li-Fraumenii syndrome in the families studied here.
the TP53 gene accounts for a significant proportion of the Li-Fraumenie syndrome cases and the other genes are less frequently mutated.
the genes PTEN and p16 are unlikely to be the cause of Li-Fraumenie Syndrome.
